<h1 align="center">Castaway</h1>

<p align="center">
  <b>Ten hours on one tiny island. Almost nothing happens, polished to a high shine.</b><br>
  <sub>A demo logo is the thing you stare at while you wait. Castaway is ten hours of waiting, so it got a proper one.</sub>
</p>

Castaway (working title) is a stationary-frame lo-fi video for YouTube, in the spirit of the ten-hour lofi streams: a young woman alone on a tiny island with one tall palm, a raft and a lot of time. She mostly idles, nodding to the music on her headphones, and every so often something happens. A message in a bottle washes up and goes straight back out. A delivery drone drops off a parcel, and the parcel is another pair of headphones. A coconut falls on a hermit crab, then walks off with the crab inside. It is an unofficial remake, inspired by the small-island routines and visual comedy of *Johnny Castaway*, the 1992 desert-island screensaver, repainted as a sunny, hand-painted coastal anime scene: 16:9, 1080p, 30 fps, and always daytime.

**The schedule.** More than 90 activities live in [activities.toml](activities.toml), on four timers: everyday routines every 2 to 5 minutes, small gags every 12 to 25, set pieces every 30 to 60, and super-rare callbacks every 3 to 6 hours. Each one waits for the next bar of the music (3 seconds) before it starts, so the gags land on the beat. The glint on the logo above keeps the same rule, then waits three more bars, which is very much the house style.

**The sound.** Every sound is synthesized from code by [tools/make_audio.py](tools/make_audio.py): no samples, no loops, no recordings, so no third-party licence applies. The theme is a seamless 60-second loop at 80 BPM.

```sh
python tools/serve.py
# then open http://127.0.0.1:8765/
```

<p align="center">
  <sub>Live preview in the browser, then export a frame-exact, YouTube-ready MP4. Plain ES modules, no build step, no npm packages.<br>
  In development: no video has been published yet. For now the island only takes visitors on port 8765.</sub>
</p>

<details>
<summary><b>ONE LETTER, UP CLOSE</b>: how the logo is put together, pixel by pixel</summary>
<br>

<p align="center">
  <img src="assets/35-hand-pixelled-chrome-logo_opus_5.5-magnify.svg" width="100%" alt="The W from the Castaway logo on its own, magnified three times on a black panel with the pixel grid drawn over it, and notes on the right with leader lines to the pixels they describe: lit top edge, a white row; sky, violet to pale blue; one-pixel black outline; bands meet, checkerboard; an island in the chrome, a tiny dark palm on a mound in the W's left stem; horizon, glare and zigzag; extruded 5 px down-right; sand, dark to light. Underneath, the banner's palette in 32 slots: 29 swatches filled, from black and violets through white, reds, oranges and sand, sea blues, three cat greys and a pink, and 3 empty slots. Label: the banner's palette, 32 slots, 29 used, all 12-bit.">
</p>

**The recipe.** Between 1988 and 1993 an Amiga or Atari ST group logo was drawn dot by dot in a paint program, 320 pixels wide and in 16 or 32 colours, and chrome was the favourite finish: metal capitals reflecting an imaginary sky above a hard horizon and an imaginary desert below it, banded because the palette is tiny. This one keeps the recipe and moves the desert to the seaside. Sky from violet to pale blue, one white row of glare along a horizon that zigzags like small waves, coral and sand underneath, a one-pixel black outline, a lit top edge, a side extruded five pixels down and to the right, and white stars on the corners.

**The honest version of "hand-pixelled".** No paint program was involved. A Node script builds the capitals from chamfered rectangles, leans them one pixel every three rows, picks every pixel of a 320 by 140 buffer itself (bands, bevels, outlines, dither and all), then writes each colour out as one SVG path. Every colour is a 12-bit Amiga value, one hex digit a channel, and the script refuses to build if the banner needs more than 32 of them. It needs 29. Like the island: plenty of room, not much going on, on purpose.

**The island in the W.** Chrome reflects whatever world the artist imagines, and this one imagined a palm. Look at the W's left stem, just above the horizon. She is not on that island. She is busy.

**The cat** is the grey tabby from the stray-cat gag, which in the video arrives on a crate, climbs the palm and naps. Here it has found the T, which is flatter. It is not part of the logo, and nobody has had the heart to tell it.

```text
 THE LOGO'S TIMETABLE · 80 BPM · ONE BEAT 0.75 s · ONE BAR 3 s
 ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  stars ............ one twinkle per bar each, a beat apart
  sea .............. ripples sideways once a beat; sun glints too
  cat .............. tail flicks every 2 beats; one z every 2 beats
  glint ............ sets off on the first beat of every fourth bar,
                     takes three beats to cross, then waits
  subtitle ......... a new line every 2 bars, hard cuts
  whole picture .... one 36-second loop, no seams
  reduced motion ... holds still: big stars, no glint, line one
 ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  the video's motion defaults are hard cuts and stepped movement.
  the logo agreed to the same terms
```

The style is credited to the Amiga and Atari ST logo artists of 1988 to 1993: the Red Sector Megademo title (violet top, zigzag horizon, orange-red base), the blue-to-white-to-grey menu logo of Kefrens' Megademo 8, and the red and blue logos in Phenomena's Enigma, which Demozoo credits to Uno. Nothing of theirs is copied: no letterforms, no palette, no logos, no names. The capitals, the colours, the small font and the cat were made for this banner.

</details>

<details>
<summary><b>EVERY SO OFTEN</b>: the timers, and what turns up</summary>

```text
 EVERY SO OFTEN · THE SCHEDULE AS OF 2026-10-01
 ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  TIMER         GOES OFF EVERY      IN A TYPICAL 10-HOUR RUN
  regular       2 to 5 minutes      about 155
  occasional    12 to 25 minutes    about 30
  rare          30 to 60 minutes    about 13
  super rare    3 to 6 hours        about 2 (never more than 3)
  chained       when another says   follow-ups, on cue
 ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  more than 90 activities. counts are the median of 200 simulated
  runs. she is busy about a third of the time and idles the rest.
  every start snaps to the next bar (3 s). default run: 10:00:00,
  seed 1992, so the same seed gives the same ten hours

 ── SOME OF WHAT HAPPENS, EVENTUALLY ──────────────────────────────
  · a message in a bottle washes up and straight back out. later,
    a different bottle brings a reply
  · a delivery drone. the parcel is another pair of headphones
  · a sea turtle visits
  · a grey tabby with a white chest arrives on a crate, climbs the
    palm and naps. one day it floats off again. another day it is
    back
  · the signal hunt: one bar of signal, at the top of the palm
  · a shark in headphones nods to the beat
  · a tour boat of selfie-takers
  · a coconut falls on a hermit crab. the coconut walks off
  · she could leave any time: she walks out over the water and
    comes back with an iced coffee
  · a bro on an electric hydrofoil throws a shaka and carves off
  · bushcraft: fire by friction, a hammock, a lookout up the palm,
    spear fishing. a kumara, planted, grows through the video
  · coconut sipping, fishing, jogging laps, a sandcastle (the tide
    takes it), waving for rescue

 ── THE SCENE, WITHOUT HER ────────────────────────────────────────
  26 entries: 4 always-on effects and 22 timed events. built so
  far: shore waves and drifting cloud shadows. planned: distant
  birds, planes with vapour trails, whale pods, dolphins,
  sailboats, sandpipers, a gecko and a rain shower (a daytime one)
```

Lanes let things overlap, so a ship can sail past while she is busy with a coconut, and it even waits for her to get busy first. Run `python tools/schedule.py` to check the schedule and simulate a ten-hour run. The working notes live in [MUSING.md](MUSING.md).

</details>

  more than 150 files, every one synthesized from code: no samples,
  no loops, no recordings, so no third-party licence
  theme ....... a seamless 60 s loop: 80 BPM, F major, ii-V-I-vi,
                20 bars of exactly 3 s. electric piano, kalimba
                lead, soft drums, vinyl crackle
  ocean ....... also a seamless 60 s loop
  levels ...... -14 LUFS, true peak at or below -1 dBTP, adjustable
                in master and per routine
  reviews ..... none yet. nobody has listened to it. it has been
